Q1089704.summary: Worked in relief rather than painted flat, this darkened and cracked icon shows the Virgin turned slightly toward the Christ Child, whom she holds on her left arm, her hand gesturing toward him. The Child, in red and blue garments, sits upright with a golden halo. Venerated as the Blachernitissa, a revered image linked with the great Marian shrine of Constantinople, it was brought from Mount Athos to Moscow in 1653, where Tsar Alexis received it in person.
facts: Tradition held that the icon was made of wax mixed with the ashes of martyrs.
Recent study has found close parallels with 13th-century relief icons and a newly discovered Greek inscription, so the 13th century is now regarded as its most likely date.
It was restored by Simon Ushakov and Nikita Pavlovets in 1674 and survived the Great Fire of Moscow in 1812.
Q1089704.notes: Wikidata and Commons give '7th century', but Wikipedia reports that scholarship now favours the 13th century; whether it is the icon once kept at Blachernae is disputed (that icon is thought to have been of the Orans type, while this one is a Hodegetria). This redating moves the work out of the 1st–7th-century batch. The phrasing 'survived the Great Fire' follows Wikipedia's statement that it was left in the Kremlin and put at risk in 1812.

cur:objects-vam-hodegetria-statuette.summary: Carved fully in the round, the slender Mother of God stands holding the Christ Child on her left arm and gestures toward him with her right hand, showing him as the Way. The Child sits upright, holding a scroll and blessing. Almost unique as a freestanding Byzantine statuette, it preserves the form of the venerated Hodegetria icon in three dimensions.
facts: The V&A describes it as the sole surviving example of freestanding Byzantine ivory sculpture; it was probably placed in a small tabernacle so that it could be seen from all sides.

The head of the Christ Child is a 19th-century restoration, most probably made in the Castellani workshop in Rome; a lozenge pattern of dots on the Virgin's cloak suggests it was once painted and gilded.
It was bought from the collection of Alessandro Castellani in Rome in 1884.
